newsitem.title: UK: Marsteller Advertising sees '97 revs of $75-85 mln.
newsitem.headline: Marsteller Advertising sees '97 revs of $75-85 mln.

text.p: Marsteller Advertising, the business-to-business advertising arm of public relations firm Burson-Marsteller, said it sees 1997 revenues reaching about $75 to $85 million, as the market for corporate advertising continues to grow.

"In the U.S. we're probably $60 million, 55 to 60, and here (in Europe) this year we'll be somewhere between 20 and 25 (million dollars)," Terry Hill, chief executive officer for Marsteller Advertising, Europe, told Reuters in an interview late on Wednesday at his London office.

Marsteller Advertising, relaunched by Burson-Marsteller in 1995 to target the corporate advertising market, expects 1998 revenues to top $100 million. The 1998 figure will include an existing Burson-Marsteller unit now operating under a differnt name that is due to be wrapped into Marsteller Advertising next year, Hill said.

Burson-Marsteller, which describes itself as a "perception management firm," in 1996 had total revenues of $261 million. It did not break out separate revenues for Marsteller Advertising, but said the unit achieved double-digit growth.

Marsteller Advertising was started in the 1950s and continued to operate as a separate unit after merging with Burson Public Relations. After Burson-Marsteller was acquired by advertising agency Young & Rubicam in 1979, Marsteller Advertising was phased out because all advertising was to be handled by Young & Rubicam.
Burson-Marsteller in 1988 resurrected the concept of handling corporate advertising itself, because most business-to-business advertising accounts were too small to be of interest to Young & Rubicam.

Hill noted that Young & Rubicam typically would not pitch for corporate advertising accounts because they might be worth only $4 million, compared to the $20 million consumer advertising accounts that are the lifeblood of the agency.

In 1995 Burson-Marsteller decided to handle corporate advertising in a separate unit, relaunching the name Marsteller Advertising in the U.S. in early 1995. Marsteller Advertising started up in Europe in 1996 "in a very small way," Hill said.

Although corporate advertising had its roots in the 1950s and enjoyed a burst of growth in the 1970s. But it fell on hard times during the ensuing recession. "Corporate advertising is the easiest thing to cut," said Hill.
"If I'm doing a $10 million corporate advertising campaign and the company is having a bad year, it's easy to cut the whole thing because it does not support a product."

Corporate advertising -- which focuses on promoting a company's image to the business community, as well as advocacy and issues -- has been growing steadily since making a comeback in the 1980s, Hill said.
Corporate advertising is a less-developed market in Europe than America, but that is changing.
"It has fewer fans here, but it's coming," Hill said. "As companies decide to present themselves as multinationals, corporate advertising becomes a very good way of sowing the seeds."
And while accounts are typically smaller than consumer advertising accounts, profit margins are generally higher.
"(Margins) tend to be higher," Hill said, noting that the process of developing corporate ads is generally less involved and less time consuming than for consumer advertising.
Corporate advertising frequently needs the approval of only a company's chief executive, as opposed to the battery of staff usually involved in a company's consumer advertising.

When corporate advertising is commission-based, however, it can be less lucrative because the media buys are smaller. As a result, corporate advertising tends to be handled more often on a fee basis than a commission basis, Hill said.
